sysd-q-148.title: Dijkstra's algorithm
sysd-q-148.text: Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest paths from a source node to every other node in a weighted graph, such as a road network. It starts with distance zero at the source and infinity elsewhere. It then repeatedly picks the unvisited vertex with the lowest distance, and updates each unvisited neighbor's distance if the route through that vertex is shorter. It can stop as soon as the shortest path to one chosen destination is known. A min-priority queue selects the closest vertex, and a binary heap ({{ref:sysd-q-087}}) gives O((V+E) log V). Sparse networks such as road maps suit it. Modern routing systems pair it with preprocessing such as {{ref:sysd-q-149}} or landmark heuristics. Preprocessing with {{ref:sysd-q-150}} can be up to seven orders of magnitude faster. The algorithm gives incorrect results when edges have negative weights, because its greedy strategy finalizes a vertex's distance before a cheaper path through a negative edge is seen.

sysd-q-149.title: A* search algorithm
sysd-q-149.text: A* is Dijkstra's algorithm with a sense of direction. It is an informed, best-first search on a weighted graph that finds the cheapest path from a start node to a goal node. It keeps a tree of paths from the start and extends the one that minimizes f(n) = g(n) + h(n). Here g(n) is the cost from the start to n, and h(n) is a heuristic estimating the cheapest remaining path to the goal. On a road map the heuristic can be the straight-line distance to the goal, the physically smallest possible distance. A* returns an optimal path when the heuristic is admissible, meaning it never overestimates. Dijkstra's algorithm is the special case where h(x) = 0 for all nodes, and A* differs from greedy best-first search because it also counts the distance already travelled. A close estimate cuts node expansions and a poor one causes many. Its biggest practical drawback is that it keeps all generated nodes in memory, and in travel routing it is generally outperformed by algorithms that pre-process the graph.

sysd-q-152.title: Geocoding
sysd-q-152.text: Type an address into a map and it becomes a point on the globe. Geocoding turns a text description of a location, such as an address or place name, into geographic coordinates, usually a latitude and longitude pair. Reverse geocoding converts coordinates back to a place name or address. A geocoder combines an input dataset of descriptive text, a reference dataset of feature locations, and software that matches each input to a reference feature. Address interpolation uses street segments tagged with address ranges. The geocoder parses the address, matches a segment whose number range includes it, and estimates the position along that segment. Accuracy varies, from building centroids and interpolated street positions to postal code centroids. Misspelled or incomplete input and outdated reference data cause mismatches. Geocoders handle abbreviations such as E for East, and cleaning the input, called address scrubbing, improves accuracy. Asking for the city and region resolves ambiguity, such as the same street name in two towns. The grid-style geocode described in {{ref:sysd-reliab-005}} encodes latitude and longitude into a short alphanumeric string.

sysd-q-150.title: Contraction hierarchies
sysd-q-150.text: Dijkstra's algorithm is impractical on road networks, which have tens of millions of vertices. Contraction hierarchies are a speed-up technique that precomputes shortcuts in the road graph, so a query can skip unimportant vertices. Road networks change rarely, so seconds to hours can be spent once on preprocessing, and queries are then answered in microseconds. The idea relies on roads being highly hierarchical: highway junctions rank above a junction into a dead end. A shortcut joins two non-adjacent vertices with the weight of their shortest path. Preprocessing contracts vertices one by one. It removes a vertex and adds a shortcut between two neighbors only if their shortest path goes through it. Choosing the best contraction order is NP-complete, so heuristics are used. A query runs a bidirectional search from the start and target over the graph plus shortcuts. Both searches follow only edges to more important vertices, which keeps the search space small. If edge weights change more often than the road topology, a customization phase can include current traffic or honor preferences such as avoiding ferries or highways.

sysd-q-061.title: Map tiles
sysd-q-061.text: A map of the whole world is cut into small pieces, and your device fetches only the pieces it needs. The world's map is projected into one huge 2D image and broken into small blocks called tiles, which the client joins seamlessly into the visible map. When the user pans, most tiles stay relevant and only new ones are fetched. Zoom level 0 shows the whole world in one tile. Each level doubles both dimensions, so one tile becomes 4, and about 22 levels suffice. Web Mercator ({{ref:sysd-q-151}}) is used, with latitude limits near 85 degrees. The OpenStreetMap XYZ convention serves tiles at URLs like .../Z/X/Y.png, with Z the zoom level. Tiles are static and rarely change, so a CDN backed by cloud storage such as S3 serves them from a nearby location. Most tiles are raster images such as PNG or JPEG. Vector tiles are rendered by the client, which can style them and keep text readable when rotating.

sysd-q-151.title: Web Mercator projection
sysd-q-151.text: Virtually every major online map provider draws the world in Web Mercator, including Google Maps, Mapbox, Bing Maps and OpenStreetMap. It is a variant of the Mercator map projection that applies spherical formulas to WGS 84 coordinates, and its identifier is EPSG:3857. The spherical form makes it slightly non-conformal, but it needs only a fraction of the computing resources of the ellipsoidal one. Mercator projects the poles at infinity, so Web Mercator cannot show them. Google Maps cuts off coverage at 85.051129° north and south, the latitude at which the full map becomes a square.

sysd-q-060.title: Designing Google Maps
sysd-q-060.text:
Design a map service in the style of Google Maps, which as of March 2021 had one billion daily active users and 99% coverage of the world. A simplified design breaks into 3 high-level components: location, map rendering and navigation.

The location service records user location updates, which clients send every few seconds. That data is used to detect new and recently closed roads, to improve the map's accuracy over time, and as an input for live traffic data. The road network is modeled as a graph: intersections are vertices, road sections are edges, and edge weights are the travel time along that section. Map data can live in a spatial database, which is needed for dynamic data or a huge amount of geographic data and supports spatial queries and geometry manipulation.

For rendering, the world's map is projected into a huge 2D image and broken into tiles. Tiled web maps use Web Mercator, and Google Maps cuts coverage at 85.051129° north and south. Zoom level 0 shows the whole world in one tile and each level doubles both dimensions, so one tile becomes 4. About 22 zoom levels are sufficient for most practical purposes. Clients request tiles by URL such as .../Z/X/Y.png. On a pan most displayed tiles stay relevant and only new ones are fetched, which beats fetching one image for the whole viewport. Tiles are static and rarely change, so a CDN backed by cloud storage like S3 serves them, and users load the tiles they need from a nearby CDN. To support zooming and panning, pre-calculate the map blocks at different zoom levels and load the images when needed. Pre-computing individual tiles is easy to parallelize.

The navigation service finds a reasonably fast route from point A to point B. It calls a Geocoding Service to resolve an address to a latitude and longitude pair, and a Route Planner Service to find the route. Geocoding matches an address to a street segment whose address range includes the house number and interpolates the position within that range. The Route Planner calculates the top-K shortest paths between A and B. It estimates the time of each path from current traffic and historical data, then ranks the paths by predicted time and user filtering.

Plain Dijkstra's algorithm is impractical on networks with tens of millions of vertices. A* with a straight-line-distance heuristic helps, but it is generally outperformed by algorithms that pre-process the graph. Contraction hierarchies precompute shortcuts, spending seconds to hours once because roads change rarely. They then answer queries in microseconds with a bidirectional search that only climbs toward more important vertices. When live traffic changes edge weights more often than the road topology, a customization phase re-applies the stored contractions with new weights. It can also honor preferences such as avoiding ferries or highways. The thing to remember is the split: static tiles from a CDN draw the map, and a pre-processed graph answers the route.

sysd-q-100.title: Non-blocking algorithm
sysd-q-100.text: Locks make threads wait, and a waiting thread accomplishes nothing. An algorithm is non-blocking if the failure or suspension of any thread cannot cause the failure or suspension of another thread. It is lock-free if there is guaranteed system-wide progress and wait-free if there is also guaranteed per-thread progress, and obstruction-freedom is the weakest guarantee. Locks can cause deadlock, livelock and priority inversion, and they force a trade-off between coarse-grained locking, which limits parallelism, and error-prone fine-grained locking. Non-blocking algorithms use atomic read-modify-write primitives provided by the hardware, most notably compare-and-swap, in a carefully designed order of reads, read-modify-writes and writes. Compilers and many CPUs reorder operations unless told not to, so memory barriers are needed. A single-reader single-writer ring buffer FIFO can be implemented safely with only a memory barrier. Correct lock-free code is difficult to write, and without hard deadlines wait-free algorithms may not be worth their extra complexity.

sysd-q-095.title: Order types
sysd-q-095.text: Before an exchange can match anything, it must know what each trader asked for. Order types are the standard instructions a trader can place on a trading venue, such as market, limit and stop orders, each with its own execution rules. A market order executes immediately at the best available price and is filled as long as willing counterparties exist. It gives certainty of execution but no control over the price received, and in fast-moving markets its fill price can differ widely from the last quote. A buy limit order executes only at the limit price or lower, and a sell limit order only at the limit price or higher. The trader controls the price, but the order may never be filled. A limit order that the {{ref:sysd-q-094}} can satisfy on arrival is marketable: it may be filled in part from the book, with the rest added to the book. Fill-or-kill orders are filled completely on the first attempt or cancelled. All-or-none orders must be filled in full or not at all. Immediate-or-cancel orders execute at once but allow partial fills. A day order lasts until the end of the day's trading session. A good-til-cancelled order persists until a cancelling order, although brokers may set limits such as 90 days. A conditional order executes only when a condition is met. A stop order becomes active when the price reaches the stop price, and a stop-limit order then becomes a limit order.

sysd-q-098.title: FIX protocol
sysd-q-098.text: Both sides of a trade speak the same protocol. FIX is an electronic communications protocol for the real-time exchange of information about securities transactions and markets. It is the standard for pre-trade communications and trade execution, used by the buy side and sell side, including mutual funds, investment banks, brokers and stock exchanges. Classic FIX tagvalue messages are ASCII text. Each field is a numeric tag plus a value separated by the SOH character, so messages are self-describing. A message has a header, a body and a trailer. The FIXT session layer is a point-to-point protocol usually run over TCP, and it guarantees delivery in both directions through sequence numbers and retransmission of missed messages. For speed, Simple Binary Encoding uses native binary types in fixed positions, giving much lower latency and more deterministic performance than tagvalue. The FIXP session layer lets peers negotiate delivery guarantees: recoverable (exactly-once, with retransmission), idempotent (at-most-once) or unsequenced. Retransmission delays are often undesirable in fast markets. FAST is a binary protocol used mostly for sending multicast price data over UDP.

sysd-q-094.title: Order book
sysd-q-094.text: A stock exchange is, at heart, two lists. The order book is the list of orders that a trading venue uses to record the interest of buyers and sellers in a financial instrument. It holds one list of buy orders and one of sell orders. Each entry keeps the number of securities, the price the buyer or seller bids or asks, and some means of identifying the party. Orders at the same price sit on one price level. A {{ref:sysd-q-096}} uses the book to decide which orders can be executed. A bid equal to or higher than the lowest ask is filled at once and never joins the open book. If such crossing orders stay unmatched because of an error or a market condition, the book is said to be crossed. The highest bid and the lowest ask are the top of the book, and the difference between them is the bid-ask spread. Book depth is the number of price levels. A book can be kept to a fixed depth, with orders beyond it ignored or rejected, or hold unlimited levels.

sysd-q-097.title: Market data
sysd-q-097.text: Market data has to reach traders before the market changes. It is the price and other related data for a financial instrument, reported by a trading venue such as a stock exchange. A record carries the instrument identifier (ticker symbol and exchange code), the latest bid and ask price and the time of the last trade. Quote data and trade data are often generated over different feeds. Delivery is highly time-sensitive, so specialized ticker plants collect and push massive data streams. Distribution platforms use specially designed protocols to raise throughput or reduce latency. UDP multicast delivers data efficiently to many recipients at once, and the FAST protocol of {{ref:sysd-q-098}} exists for multicast market data. In a feed handler, sources connect to a server that redistributes data. It forwards a client's subscription to the sources if it has no cached data, then sends every update for an instrument to all subscribed clients. Reference data such as identifier codes and security terms does not change in real time and usually comes from the issuer, while prices come from the exchanges.

sysd-q-096.title: Matching engine
sysd-q-096.text: The matching engine decides who trades with whom. It is the component that uses the order book to determine which buy and sell orders can be fully or partially executed. Orders are matched as the interest of buyers and sellers can be satisfied. An order whose bid is equal to or higher than the lowest ask can be fulfilled immediately and does not become part of the open orders book. A limit order may be partially filled from the book, with the remainder added to the book. A market order may be split across several counterparties at different prices. Electronic markets give market orders the highest priority, then limit orders first-come-first-served. Conditional orders get priority by the time their condition is met, and special kinds such as iceberg and dark-pool orders get lower priority. In a low-latency exchange design the matching engine is single-threaded on the critical path and pinned to a CPU, so there is no context switch and no locks.

sysd-q-099.title: Processor affinity
sysd-q-099.text: Leaving a thread where it is can make it faster. Processor affinity, also called CPU pinning, binds a process or thread to a CPU or a range of CPUs so that it executes only on the designated processors. A thread that resumes on its old CPU may find data still in that CPU's cache and take fewer cache misses. But pinning forces it to wait for that CPU to become free. It suits CPU-intensive processes with few interrupts, while an ordinary program that is interrupted more often might be slowed down. On Linux it is set with the taskset program or the sched_setaffinity system call.

sysd-q-028.title: Low-latency critical path design
sysd-q-028.text: A modern stock exchange reaches microsecond latency with one principle: do less on the critical path. That means fewer tasks, less time on each task, fewer network hops and less disk usage. Non-critical tasks leave the path. The market data flow and the reporting flow are off it and have different latency requirements. Key components can be single-threaded, each pinned to a CPU as in {{ref:sysd-q-099}}, with no context switch and no locks. Each runs one task after another in a single loop. Components can talk through shared memory as an event bus instead of a hard disk, and run together on one giant server without containers.

sysd-q-027.title: Designing a stock exchange
sysd-q-027.text:
Design a stock exchange, a system whose aim is microsecond latency. It gets there by doing less on the critical path: fewer tasks, less time on each task, fewer network hops and less disk usage. The trading flow is that critical path, with strict latency requirements. An order enters the order manager, passes mandatory risk checks and is matched, and the execution leaves through the order manager. The market data flow and the reporting flow are not on the critical path and have different latency requirements, so non-critical tasks are removed from the trading flow.

Clients send orders, instructions to buy or sell, to a broker or directly to the exchange. FIX, the standard protocol for pre-trade communications and trade execution, carries them as numeric tag and value fields. FIX sessions use sequence numbers and retransmission on request, so delivery survives a disconnection. High-performance sessions can instead pick idempotent or unsequenced delivery, since retransmission delays are often undesirable in fast markets. Binary encodings such as Simple Binary Encoding cut latency, because no translation is needed to put data into a format computers can use. Fixed-length fields make performance more deterministic.

A market order executes at once at the best available price, giving certainty of execution but no price control. A limit order executes only at its limit price or better and may never fill. Time-in-force and conditional instructions add rules. Day orders expire at the session close, good-til-cancelled orders persist, immediate-or-cancel allows partial fills, and a stop order activates at its stop price. The order book is the data model. It is a list of buy orders and a list of sell orders. Each entry holds the party, the number of securities and the price, and orders at one price are grouped into a price level. The top of the book is the highest bid and lowest ask, their gap is the bid-ask spread, and book depth is the number of price levels kept.

The matching engine uses the book to decide which orders can be fully or partially executed. A bid at or above the lowest ask fills at once, and a partly filled limit order rests on the book. Matching priority favors market orders, then limit orders first-come-first-served, with conditional orders ranked by when their condition is met and iceberg or dark-pool orders lower. Market data, the latest bid, ask and last trade, is published off the critical path. Its delivery is highly time-sensitive, ticker plants handle the streams, and UDP multicast serves many recipients at once.

All components run on a single giant server with no containers, and shared memory serves as the event bus with no hard disk. Other components listen on the bus and react, in the event-driven style of {{ref:sysd-msg-020}}. The order manager and matching engine are single-threaded on the critical path, and each is pinned to a CPU. There is no context switch and no locks, and the loop runs tasks one by one in sequence. Locks block threads and risk deadlock and priority inversion, so the design avoids them in shared structures. Lock-free data structures raise parallel performance, and a single-reader single-writer ring buffer needs only a memory barrier. The thing to remember is that speed here comes from removing work: fewer tasks, fewer hops and less disk on the critical path.

sysd-q-146.title: Collaborative real-time editing
sysd-q-146.text: Two people type into the same document at the same moment, and both must see the result. Collaborative real-time editing lets several users edit the same document at once on different devices, with their edits merged automatically and nearly instantly. It synchronizes the edits of all online users automatically and periodically, which avoids or minimizes edit conflicts. Asynchronous editing, delayed or offline, makes each user submit, update and merge manually, so several users can edit the same line and cause conflicts. The difficulty is communication latency. Users need their own edits incorporated instantly, yet instant incorporation means edits land in different versions of the document. If Bob turns Mary into Hary while Alice turns it into My, each receives edits made on versions that never existed locally. The most sophisticated solutions need no server and no locking, so all users edit all parts at once. A basic client-server design instead makes one editor the collaboration server, which is less powerful but cheap. A sequence CRDT can serve as an alternative to {{ref:sysd-q-145}}.

sysd-q-147.title: Groupware concurrency control
sysd-q-147.text: Concurrency control for groupware has unusual demands. Groupware is a computer system that supports two or more users working on a common task through a shared environment. Such systems often require fine-granularity sharing of data and fast response times. A paper on the topic separates real-time groupware from other multi-user systems and sets out their requirements. It presents a concurrency control algorithm that is simple to use and responsive, because users operate directly on the data without obtaining locks. The paper applies it to group text editing and notes that the behavior wanted in many such systems is non-serializable.

sysd-q-145.title: Operational transformation
sysd-q-145.text: Operational transformation repairs edits that arrive out of context. It is a technique for keeping replicated documents consistent under concurrent edits by transforming each operation's parameters against the effects of concurrent operations already executed. Ellis and Gibbs pioneered it in 1989 for collaborative editing of plain text. In 2009 it was adopted as a core technique behind Google Wave and Google Docs. Each client holds its own copy and edits it without locking or blocking. Changes are propagated, and each receiver transforms them before executing. Take the text abc, with O1 = insert x at 0 and O2 = delete c at 2. Untransformed, O2 would delete b instead of c, so after O1 it must become delete at 3. The goals are causality preservation, which keeps operations in cause-effect order, and convergence, which makes all copies identical once all operations have run. The CCI model adds intention preservation. OT is hard to get right: formal proofs are complicated and error-prone, and a former Google Wave engineer found implementing it painful. Differential synchronization and sequence CRDTs are alternatives.

sysd-q-059.title: Designing Google Docs
sysd-q-059.text:
Design a collaborative document editor in the style of Google Docs. The system must merge edits from different users on different devices automatically and almost instantly. Real-time groupware needs fine-granularity sharing of data and fast response times. The groupware concurrency algorithm of Ellis and colleagues is simple and responsive: users operate directly on the data without obtaining locks.

Clients send document editing operations to a WebSocket server, which handles the real-time communication. Document operations are persisted in a message queue, and the file operation server consumes them and generates transformed operations using collaboration algorithms. Three types of data are stored: file metadata, file content and operations.

One of the biggest challenges is real-time conflict resolution. Users need their own edits shown instantly, but because of network latency those edits are applied to different versions of the document. If Bob turns Mary into Hary while Alice turns it into My, each receives edits made against versions that never existed locally. Remote edits must still be applied despite conflicts with local ones.

Common conflict-resolution algorithms are operational transformation (OT), differential synchronization (DS) and conflict-free replicated data types (CRDT). With OT each client holds its own replica and edits it without locks. It transforms changes received from others before executing them, which suits high-latency environments such as the web. OT adjusts an operation's parameters for concurrent operations already executed. Untransformed, deleting position 2 would delete b instead of c, so after inserting x at position 0 of abc it must become position 3. OT must keep causality, with operations executing in their cause-effect order, and convergence, with all copies identical once every operation has run. Intention preservation is a further goal.

OT is hard to get right. Formal proofs are complicated and error-prone, a former Google Wave engineer found implementing it painful, and every change to the data must be captured. A sequence CRDT can build a collaborative real-time editor as an alternative, and differential synchronization is another. Google Docs is said to use OT, which was adopted in 2009 as a core technique behind Google Wave and Google Docs. CRDT remains an active research area. A basic alternative is a client-server model where one editor acts as the collaboration server, though changes may not show on a client until the server answers. It is less powerful but cheap, suiting limited processing resources. The thing to remember is that operations flow through a queue, and transformation is what keeps every copy of the document the same.

openers.design-google-maps: As of March 2021 Google Maps had one billion daily active users and 99% coverage of the world. A simplified design breaks into 3 high-level components: location, map rendering and navigation. Navigation leans on shortest-path algorithms, from Dijkstra's algorithm and the A* search to contraction hierarchies, which precompute shortcuts so a query can skip unimportant vertices. Rendering rests on map tiles, a world map projected into one huge 2D image and cut into small blocks, in Web Mercator, the standard projection for web mapping. Geocoding, which turns an address into a latitude and longitude pair, connects the two.
openers.design-a-stock-exchange: A stock exchange records the interest of buyers and sellers in an order book, and a matching engine uses that book to decide which orders can be executed. Traders place orders of standard types such as market, limit and stop. The aim is microsecond latency, reached by doing less on the critical path: fewer tasks, less time on each task, fewer network hops and less disk usage. This chapter covers the parts, from FIX, the electronic protocol for the real-time exchange of information about securities transactions, and market data to processor affinity and non-blocking algorithms. Then it assembles them in one design.
openers.design-google-docs: Two people can edit the same document at once, on different devices, and the system must merge their edits automatically and almost instantly. Real-time groupware needs fine-granularity sharing of data and fast response times. This chapter starts with collaborative real-time editing and the concurrency control that groupware needs. Then it turns to operational transformation, a technique for keeping replicated documents consistent under concurrent edits. The worked design puts these ideas into one service.

reviews.design-google-maps: The chapter splits a map into a picture and a route. For the picture, Web Mercator flattens the world, map tiles cut it into blocks, and a CDN serves them from nearby. For the route, Dijkstra's algorithm gives shortest paths, A* adds a heuristic estimate, and contraction hierarchies precompute shortcuts so queries answer in microseconds. Geocoding sits between them, turning an address into the coordinates that the route needs. The worked design adds a location service, whose updates help detect new and closed roads and feed live traffic data, and arranges everything in three components.
reviews.design-a-stock-exchange: Every part of the chapter serves the critical path. Order types say what traders ask for, FIX carries those orders in, and the order book holds them until the matching engine pairs buyers and sellers. Market data and reporting stay off the critical path. To keep the path fast, the matching engine runs single-threaded and pinned to a CPU, using processor affinity and non-blocking techniques rather than locks. The worked design puts it all on one server with shared memory as an event bus.
reviews.design-google-docs: The chapter starts from a problem: latency means edits land on different versions of the document. Groupware concurrency control answers with an algorithm that lets users work on the data without locks. Operational transformation makes that practical by adjusting each operation's parameters against concurrent ones, so every copy converges. The worked design sends operations through a WebSocket server and a message queue to a file operation server, and it names CRDTs and differential synchronization as alternatives.
